doc.title: John LaPorta interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 13, 1996

title: Writing for Artie Shaw, education publishing and the school jazz band series
summary: His Artie Shaw band writing met resistance, he formed an experimental band, then wrote for Kendor, Marshall Brown and Berklee, including a twenty-two volume project.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Tell me about your composing and arranging over the years. You’ve written some stage band material, you’ve got books out.

Well originally I was writing and got calls to write for different, I wrote for Artie Shaw, it was called the “Million Dollar Band.” And that was quite an experience. Because I didn’t write the way the musicians were used to hearing it, and it wasn’t like Basie where everybody played together you know. It had individual parts. One piece was called the “Growth of an Idea” and there were seven different lines you know, so everybody in the band had to play. And unfortunately in big bands there is always a bunch of dead wood in it, see? And I knew instantly the problems that that band had. But they were at a furor about it see, and that was quite traumatic for me. So in the South of France, I wound up because of the rejects over a period of time, developing an experimental band and I had that, we used to rehearse weekly for, and played two or three different concerts, that’s all, in that time for about five or six years. But it was mainly for me to find out. And I did find out that they were partially right that I had to restructure the way I wrote, strengthen lines and things of that nature. I didn’t change essentially the direction of it, but I learned

how to cope with it better, realistically, in terms of what people could do. And then I got into writing for jazz education. Art Dedrick, who was the founder of Kendor Music in New York, sounded me about it. He was I think the first one to start publishing for it. He was an arranger for one of the radio stations in Buffalo. And he sounded me about it and I got involved with that and then later on I was doing some for Marshall Brown and then for Berklee a great deal once I went there. In fact I was working on a major work when I went there, a twenty-two volume work developing the school jazz band. And you know for eight brass, five saxes and rhythm section and also some alternate instruments, clarinet, flute, French horn, I think tuba too, and a conductor. And that was a five year project for me.
That sounds like a big project.
Oh it was. I had to forego the writing that I was doing pretty much, to get it done.
